## Purpose

<!-- hand:purpose -->
> Draft — owner review pending.

The endocrine, metabolic and temperature model: stress hormones (sympathetic activity, adrenaline, noradrenaline,
cortisol), glucose and insulin, thyroid state, the system-level conditions (sepsis, anaphylaxis, SIRS, hypermetabolic
states, thyroid storm), whole-body heat balance and malignant hyperthermia. It is stepped at 1 Hz and mostly hands
multipliers to the circulation, the lungs and the gas model rather than values to display. A clinician-educator can read
here why a patient cools under anaesthesia, warms in MH, turns hyperglycaemic after incision or vasoplegic in sepsis; an
embedding developer can see which commands (`stimulus`, `meal`, the thermal and condition commands) reach it.
<!-- /hand:purpose -->

## Equations in words

<!-- hand:equations -->
> Draft — owner review pending.

- Heat balance: two compartments, core two thirds and periphery one third of body mass at 3.5 kJ/kg/°C. The core gains
  metabolic heat and warm-fluid heat and loses heat to the periphery and the airway; the periphery gains heat from the
  core and forced air and loses dry, skin-evaporative and sweat heat (`l2/thermal/heat.ts`).
- Metabolic heat is the resting rate, reduced under general anaesthesia in proportion to the thermoregulatory depth
  (capped at 1), plus shivering, MH muscle heat and the thyroid/sepsis multipliers (`l2/thermal/heat.ts`). Heat is
  oxidative (E131): the resting, thyroid/sepsis and shivering heat are multiplied by the share of the oxygen demand the
  circulation delivers (the blood model's achieved ÷ demanded VO2: 1 above the critical delivery, falling to 0 with no
  flow), so a body in cardiac arrest makes no oxidative heat. Anaerobic glycolysis is not counted (about 98 kJ per mol
  lactate; the lactate model has no substrate or pH limit, so counting it would heat a body without flow) — a known
  under-count.
- Core-to-periphery conductance is a logistic function of core temperature around the vasoconstriction threshold,
  between a constricted and a dilated value (`l2/thermal/params.ts`). E131: the part above tissue conduction
  (5.28 W/m²/°C × body surface area, the Gagge 1971 two-node model's core–skin K) is carried by skin blood flow, so it
  is multiplied by a skin-perfusion FLOW fraction: cardiac output ÷ the output at which a normally oxygenated patient's
  delivery becomes critical (about 40 % of resting output; hypoxaemia and anaemia do not shut the skin). With no flow
  only conduction through tissue remains.
- Sweating and shivering need the hypothalamic efferent (E131): both are multiplied by the vasomotor centre's
  brain-perfusion gate — the baroreflex's own `brainstemOutF(cbfRel)`, 1 at ≥ 0.6 of normal cerebral flow and 0 at
  0.2 (Astrup 1981 thresholds) — so they stop when the brain is unperfused; there is no "dead" flag. Measured
  (`thermal-mh-arrest-heat.test.ts`, 70 kg, 21 °C, ventilated): VF at 38.55 °C, then 37.59 °C one hour later
  (0.96 °C/h; the brief's forensic rule of thumb 0.5–1.5 °C/h; Henssge's nomogram formula would give a plateau of only
  0.15 °C in that first hour — the 2-node model has no plateau). Before E131 the same body fell 3.8 °C in the hour
  because sweating and the dilated core–skin transfer kept running.
- Thresholds: anaesthesia widens the interthreshold range linearly in depth, from awake sweat 37.2 / vasoconstriction
  36.9 / shivering 36.0 °C to GA 38.0 / 34.5 / 33.5 °C, extrapolated beyond depth 1 and clamped at 1.5 (Sessler
  2008/2016; `tables §5c`; `l2/thermal/thresholds.ts`).
- Dry skin loss is radiation plus convection through an insulation layer, with h_r = 4·ε·σ·f_rad·T̄³ and
  h_c = 10.3·v^0.6 (Pulse's forms with consistent units); the insulation is calibrated at creation so the awake patient
  at 21 °C is in balance (`l2/thermal/environment.ts`; NOTICES N-P17).
- Temperature sites follow core with a first-order lag, from oesophageal (τ 45 s) to rectal (τ 40 min); axilla reads
  0.5 °C low (`l2/thermal/heat.ts`).
- MH: muscle activity = severity × an onset ramp (full over 15 min) × the fraction not suppressed by dantrolene; that
  fraction relaxes towards 1 − gain × the drug model's dantrolene effect, so the crisis can recrudesce as the drug
  wanes (`l2/thermal/mh.ts`).
- MH metabolism is ONE rate (E131): the hypermetabolic muscle adds an oxygen demand M_mh = activity ×
  (2.5 − 1) × the resting VO2 (whole-body VO2 × 2.5 at full fulminant activity: tables §5.3 "×2–3"; swine ≈ × 2,
  Gronert & Theye 1976, Gronert 1977/1986), and everything derives from it: the VO2 demand is basal + M_mh; the CO2 is
  the achieved part × the muscle's RQ 0.97 (Cooper 1992) plus 22 mL CO2 per mmol of the MH muscle's anaerobic lactate
  as bicarbonate buffers it (Beaver, Wasserman & Whipp 1986); the heat is the achieved part × the caloric equivalent of
  oxygen at that RQ, 21.1 kJ/L (Weir 1949); the lactate is the unmet demand through the blood model's existing
  delivery-limited pathway; the potassium efflux follows the same activity. "Achieved" is the blood model's delivered
  share of the demand, so with no flow none of it happens. Dantrolene lowers the activity and everything falls
  together. The old three independent factors (heat × 8 basal, VO2 × 2.5, VCO2 × 3) are gone: they made 640 W of heat
  from oxygen worth about 120 W (`l2/thermal/metabolic.ts`, `l2/thermal/heat.ts`, `l2/resp/pipeline.ts`,
  `l2/blood/pipeline.ts`).
- What that means for the course (measured on the MH card, 80 kg, untreated, constant ventilation): EtCO2 95 mmHg at
  +15 min (E129: 72), pH 7.04, lactate rising to 20+; the MH heat is about 140 W, so the core rises about 0.12 °C per
  5 min and plateaus near 38.6 °C once sweating starts — there is no hyperthermic VF (E129's arrest at 42.3 °C came from
  the 640 W). The "+1 °C per 5–15 min" of tables §7 check 21 needs 270–550 W of net heat into 70–80 kg, 2–4 × what the
  sourced VO2 multiple can make: it is kept as a known miss, not tuned.
- MH tachycardia (E117, rc.4). The MH's sympathetic drive is front-loaded: it approaches 2.5 × severity (in units of
  stress activity) with τ 2 min from the trigger, instead of following the 15-min metabolic ramp (the old coupling was
  2 × the metabolic activity), and it falls with dantrolene's suppression on the same 2-min τ while the metabolic
  excess keeps its 10-min τ. So the heart rate is rising before the EtCO2 leaves its baseline: tachycardia is among
  the earliest and most consistent signs of MH (Miller's Anesthesia 10e, malignant hyperthermia chapter; Larach 2010),
  and plasma catecholamines rise many-fold in porcine MH, as a consequence of the hypermetabolism (Gronert, Milde &
  Theye, Anesthesiology 1977); the 2-min τ and the 2.5 are engineered to the owner's target.
- Hypercapnia raises sympathetic activity by 0.03 per mmHg of PaCO2 above 45, up to 0.3 at 55 (the chemoreflex:
  hypercapnia raises muscle sympathetic nerve activity in conscious humans, Somers et al., J Appl Physiol 1989; its
  heart-rate arm and its size under anaesthesia are engineered). It is kept small because the adrenal hypercapnia
  drive and the circulation's chemoreflex pressor term (both above PaCO2 50) already answer the same stimulus — a known
  overlap for the owner — and, being a central chemoreflex, it is scaled by the vasomotor centre's perfusion gate and by the
  anaesthetic's sympatholysis, both the baroreflex's own (propofol suppresses MSNA: Ebert et al., Anesthesiology 1992). The metabolic acidaemia is not a second input (the central chemoreceptors track PaCO2; a carotid
  metabolic-H+ term would move the sepsis, DKA and haemorrhage HR bands).
- The hypermetabolic MH muscle dilates its own vessels (metabolic hyperaemia): SVR × (1 − 0.2 × MH activity), as the
  thyroid storm's hypermetabolism already lowers SVR. Without it the larger sympathetic drive raised the untreated
  MAP at +20 min from 99 to 115 against the FU-7.1 band (≤ 104); with it 101, and the pressure still peaks and falls
  back as the pH does. The MH potassium efflux is 2.35 (was 2.2) so the larger catecholamine surge's β2 uptake keeps
  K 5.5–6.5 at 20 min.
- Measured on the showcase-mh induction at constant ventilation: HR 80 → 94 when the EtCO2 is 3 mmHg above its
  baseline (2.7 min; the same induction without MH: 74), 126 when the EtCO2 passes 55 mmHg (target ≥ 120; it was 99).
  Without MH, hypoventilation to PaCO2 51 adds 2 bpm (limit 10) and to PaCO2 68 adds 16 (the old engine 13; limit
  20). After dantrolene and doubled ventilation the HR falls from a peak of 169 to 114 at +20 min (−32 %), under the
  target audit's ceiling of 123 for an uncooled patient at 40.1 °C (row 133 band (b)). One guard band now misses:
  dantrolene's 10-min EtCO2 effect is −4.6 mmHg against ≤ −5 (−5.5 before; an it.fails in drug-layer-guards). The
  volatile's sympatholysis acts on the baroreflex as before (`l2/thermal/mh.ts` `mhSympDrive`, `l2/endo/core.ts`,
  `l2/endo/params.ts`).
- Glucose: the Bergman minimal model for disposal with Pulse's insulin secretion line, secretion ∝ (5.357·G − 328.56)
  above 80 mg/dL and zero below; endogenous production is scaled by stress, counter-regulation below 70 mg/dL and liver
  function (`l2/endo/glucose.ts`; `tables §5c`; NOTICES N-P18).
- Stress hormones: sympathetic stress activity = noxious input × (1 − antinociception) plus condition drives (onset τ
  25 s, offset τ 3 min); endogenous adrenaline = basal × (1 + 3 × adrenal drive) with t½ ≈ 2 min; noradrenaline =
  basal × (1 + 1.5 × stress activity); cortisol rises towards 400 × (1 + 2.75 × surgical drive) nmol/L with τ 1.5 h
  (`l2/endo/hormones.ts`; `tables §5c`).
- Hormones act as multipliers on the circulation's set points; exogenous adrenaline's haemodynamic effect stays the drug
  model's and is never applied twice (`l2/endo/effects.ts`; Clutter 1980 thresholds).
- Conditions interpolate their multipliers from the table columns by a continuous stage or grade, smoothed with their
  own onset τ (sepsis 600 s by default, anaphylaxis 120 s on the Ring–Messmer grades); adrenaline's β2 effect suppresses
  anaphylactic mediator release (`l2/endo/conditions.ts`; `tables §5e`). Thyroid storm adds HR 110–150, Ees × 1.3,
  SVR × 0.6, VO2 × 1.3–1.8 and core 38.5–41 °C (Klein 2007; `l2/endo/thyroid.ts`).

| `SYMP_HYPERCAPNIA_FROM_MMHG` | `45` | mmHg | Physiol 1989; Somers 1989; Anesthesiology 1992; [P: the direction of the VASCULAR sympathetic outflow, in conscious subjects]; [ENG]; [P direction] | E117: hypercapnia raises NEURAL sympathetic activity — the chemoreflex. In conscious humans breathing CO2 to raise end-tidal PCO2 by ≈ 10 mmHg, muscle sympathetic nerve activity rose markedly while the pressure rose a few mmHg (Somers VK, Mark AL, Zavala DC, Abboud FM. Contrasting effects of hypoxia and hypercapnia on ventilation and sympathetic activity in humans. J Appl Physiol 1989;67:2101–2106) [P: the direction of the VASCULAR sympathetic outflow, in conscious subjects]. Here `symp` gains SYMP_HYPERCAPNIA_PER_MMHG per mmHg of PaCO2 above SYMP_HYPERCAPNIA_FROM_MMHG, up to SYMP_HYPERCAPNIA_MAX (reached at PaCO2 55). `symp` also acts on HR, contractility and venous tone: those arms, the size, and the size under anaesthesia (volatiles blunt the reflex) are [ENG]. This is the engine's ONE neural hypercapnic sympathetic limb. Beside it only the ADRENAL hypercapnia drive (DRIVE_HYPERCAPNIA_PER_MMHG, above 50) answers the same stimulus, and that is the humoral arm, not the neural one. The circulation's own hypercapnic pressor multiplier (circ `chemoFactors`, +1 %/mmHg HR and SVR above 50, capped 20 %) was REMOVED on 2026-10-28: it had the wrong sign (CO2's direct vascular action is a VASODILATION and its direct myocardial action a depression — circ `co2VascularF`, blood `chemistryContractility`), and it carried neither sympatholysis nor the responsiveness scaling that this term carries (audit §2.5). Measured without MH: PaCO2 51 adds 2–3 bpm (limit 10); PaCO2 ≈ 68 adds ≈ 16 bpm where the old engine added 13 (limit 20); an uncapped 0.06/mmHg term gave +30 bpm at 68. (The tamponade showcase's post-ROSC systolic peak, 155 → 199, is NOT changed by the cap: 200 uncapped.) Moving this limb into the baroreflex's own sympathetic error, so that one efferent carries both afferents, was tried on 2026-10-28 and NOT shipped: the error is in mmHg of pressure and its gains were set for pressure defence, so the MSNA percent the chemoreflex is sized in (Somers 1989/1991) has no determinate exchange rate with it — see the audit §2.5 note of that date for the measured numbers. The metabolic acidaemia is NOT a second input: the central chemoreceptors track PaCO2 (the blood–brain barrier delays a metabolic H+ signal); the carotid bodies do sense metabolic H+, but such a term would move the sourced sepsis/DKA/haemorrhage HR bands the circulation already meets. The term is a CENTRAL chemoreflex: the endocrine adapters scale it by the vasomotor centre's perfusion gate (`brainstemOutF(cbfRel)`, the baroreflex's own), so the CO2 retained during an arrest does not drive it while the brainstem is unperfused — and by the anaesthetic's sympatholysis, the drug model's delivered- output factor (`ext.drug.symp`) that already scales the baroreflex's sympathetic output: propofol and the volatiles suppress muscle sympathetic nerve activity (Ebert TJ, Muzi M, Berens R, Goff D, Kampine JP, Anesthesiology 1992;76:725–733, propofol) [P direction]. Without it the CO2 a fentanyl-premedicated patient retains propped the propofol induction pressure and broke the FU-7.1 opioid-synergy band (ratio 1.13 against ≥ 1.15; main 1.16). |

Every term is a power in W. The dry skin loss is radiation + convection through an insulation layer (clothes, blankets, drapes): q_dry = A_exposed·(Tp − Ta)/(R_ins + 1/(h_r + h_c)), h_r = 4·ε·σ·f_rad·T̄³, h_c = 10.3·v^0.6 (Pulse) The insulation R_ins is CALIBRATED at creation so the awake patient at 21 °C loses exactly Stage 3's heat (so every Stage 3 number is reproduced), and every later change (ambient, air speed, exposure, forced air, ventilation, cold fluid) acts through the physical terms relative to that calibration. | `MH_VO2_PEAK_X` | `2.5` | — | tables §5.3; Anesthesiology 1976; Anesthesiology 1986; Rep 2001; [TXT]; [P abstracts; no human calorimetry found] | --- MH and dantrolene (tables §5.3, §7 check 21) ----------------------------------------------------------- E131: THE one MH rate. The hypermetabolic skeletal muscle adds an O2 demand of a(t)·(MH_VO2_PEAK_X − 1)·VO2rest (metabolic.ts `mhO2Demand`); oxygen demand, CO2, heat and lactate all derive from it (the old three independent factors MH_HEAT_X 8, MH_VO2_FACTOR 2.5 and MH_VCO2_FACTOR 3 are gone: 640 W of heat came from oxygen worth ≈ 120 W). MH_VO2_PEAK_X is the whole-body VO2 at full fulminant activity ÷ the resting VO2. Range 2–3 (tables §5.3 "VO2 ×2–3" [TXT]); the centre 2.5 is taken. Measured in swine with constant ventilation and no treatment: whole-body VO2 "almost twofold", hind-limb muscle VO2 almost threefold (Gronert GA, Theye RA, Anesthesiology 1976;44:36–43); 6.5 → 11.6 mL/kg/min, × 1.8 (Gronert GA et al., Anesthesiology 1986;64:24–28); the muscle's increase extrapolated to the whole musculature ≈ the whole-body increase, ≈ 6 mL/kg/min (Gronert GA, Heffron JJ, Milde JH, Theye RA, Can Anaesth Soc J 1977;24:103–109) — on a human 3.5 mL/kg/min resting VO2 that is × 2.7. A review gives "5-fold" as the upper extreme (Nelson TE, Biosci Rep 2001;21:169–179) [P abstracts; no human calorimetry found]. |
| `MH_RQ` | `0.97` | — | Physiol 1992; Gronert & Theye 1976; [P abstracts] | E131: respiratory quotient of the hypermetabolic muscle's oxidation. The muscle substrate RQ during exercise with glycogen available is 0.95 (ramp V-slope below the threshold) to 0.99 (steady state) (Cooper CB, Beaver WL, Cooper DM, Wasserman K, Exp Physiol 1992;77:51–64); centre 0.97. MH muscle is glycogenolytic (lactate rises first and is non-hypoxic in origin: Gronert & Theye 1976) [P abstracts]. |
| `WEIR_KCAL_PER_L_O2` | `3.941` | — | Physiol 1949; Curtin & Woledge 1978; Woledge & Reilly 1988; Prampero 1999; Anaesth 1976 | E131: the caloric equivalent of oxygen, Weir JB de V, J Physiol 1949;109:1–9: energy (kcal) = 3.941·VO2 + 1.106·VCO2 (L), i.e. 4.184·(3.941 + 1.106·RQ) kJ per L O2 — 20.2 kJ/L at the resting RQ 0.8, 21.1 at MH_RQ. The MH muscle heat is the ACHIEVED MH VO2 × this (heat.ts). Anaerobic glycolysis is not counted: per ATP it releases about as much heat as oxidation (glycogenolysis 65 vs oxidation 72 kJ/mol ATP, Curtin & Woledge 1978 and Woledge & Reilly 1988 as cited in muscle-energetics work), but it makes only 1.5 ATP per lactate, ≈ 98 kJ/mol lactate (di Prampero 1999's in-vivo estimate 84 kJ/mol) — and the blood model's lactate production has no substrate or pH limit, so counting it would heat a body with no flow without end. A known under-count (Hall GM et al., Br J Anaesth 1976;48:305–308: in porcine MH the heat is largely aerobic early; terminally aerobic metabolism accounts for about half of the muscle's temperature rise). |

Tachycardia is among the earliest and most consistent signs of MH (Miller's Anesthesia 10e, malignant hyperthermia chapter; Larach MG et al., Anesth Analg 2010;110:498–507), and in porcine MH the plasma catecholamines rise many-fold, as a consequence of the hypermetabolism rather than its cause (Gronert GA, Milde JH, Theye RA, Anesthesiology 1977;47:411–415) [TXT direction].
